newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Seoul stocks end down on weak won, Han Joo default.
newsitem.headline: Seoul stocks end down on weak won, Han Joo default.

text.p: Stocks ended lower on Monday as the won's fall against dollar and financial troubles at textile maker Han Joo dampened sentiment, brokers said.
The composite index lost 1.12 points to close at 747.29.

"A technical rebound was expected after a fall in the past four trading days, but the won's depreciation despite the central bank's dollar-selling intervention and the troubles at Han Joo chilled sentiment again," said Lee Moo-il of LG Securities.
The Korea Stock Exchange on Monday suspended trading of Han Joo after the company defaulted on its loan repayments.
An exchange official said Han Joo was believed to have suffered from financial troubles after it diversified into other businesses, including information technology.
Trading volume was very low with 28.98 million shares changing hands, against 20.97 million in Saturday's half session. Losers outpaced gainers 484 to 282 with 138 unchanged.
In addition to the won's fall, -- it ended at 898.80 after opening at 895.00 -- rising interest rates also eroded investor confidence.
Yields on three-year corporate bonds, South Korea's benchmark interest rate, currently hover at about 12.20 percent.
KEPCO rose 300 won to 26,100 thanks to foreign buying, prompted by the belief that the stock was over sold.
"The share faced profit-taking last week because of its poor performance in the first half. Now it is recovering," said Choo Hee-yup of Dongwon Securities.
Shares with good first-half results, including LG Metals, fared well.
LG Metals gained 100 won to 18,300 with 302,090 shares traded, and Samsung Heavy rose 200 won to 10,900.
Korea First Bank was also heavily traded with a volume of 545,700 shares, as foreign buying offset local institutional sales. The bank fell 20 won to 3,610.
Brokers said foreigners thought the worst was over for Korea First Bank.
